set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set1.q: What causes most acute pericarditis?
opts: Most follow myocardial infarction
Infarction is one cause rather than the commonest. Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic, and most of that is viral.
Most are idiopathic
Correct. The two statements sit together: unexplained in the sense that nothing is identified, but viral in most of those cases. Most of those are viral.
Most follow cardiac surgery
Surgery is one cause rather than the commonest. Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic, and most of those cases are viral.
Most are bacterial
Viral causes predominate among the idiopathic majority, which is itself most of acute pericarditis.

set1.io: Review the different lipoproteins
set1.q: Which lipoprotein carries the highest risk, and why?
opts: High density lipoprotein, because it is high in cholesterol
High density lipoprotein decreases risk; it carries cholesterol back to the liver.
Low density lipoprotein, because it is high in cholesterol
Correct. The composition is what determines the risk, which is why the lipoproteins are not interchangeable even though all of them carry lipid.
Very low density lipoprotein, because it is high in cholesterol
Very low density lipoprotein increases risk, but it is high in triglycerides rather than cholesterol.
All lipoproteins carry equal risk
They differ by composition, and their effect on risk differs with it.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
set1.q: Which are given as uncommon causes of coronary heart disease?
opts: Coronary vasospasm and thrombosis
These are common mechanisms acting on a narrowed vessel rather than the uncommon causes.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia and high fat diet
These are mechanisms of abnormal lipid metabolism contributing to atherosclerosis, not the uncommon causes listed.
Reduced oxygen content of the blood, and poor perfusion
Correct. Both reach the same endpoint from outside the coronary artery: the vessel may be open, but what flows through it either carries too little oxygen or arrives at too low a pressure.
Rheumatic fever and infective endocarditis
These damage valves rather than causing coronary heart disease.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coronary syndromes
set1.q: Why is unstable angina included among the acute coronary syndromes?
opts: It always involves complete vessel occlusion
Complete occlusion is not what defines it. It is grouped with the acute syndromes because it may progress to acute ischaemia.
It is caused by vasospasm rather than plaque
Vasospasm is the mechanism of Prinzmetal angina. Unstable angina is grouped as acute because it may progress.
It may progress to acute ischaemia
Correct. It is grouped by where it is heading rather than by where it currently is, which is the point of treating it as acute.
It occurs only in patients with prior infarction
Prior infarction does not define it; it is included among the acute syndromes because it may progress to acute ischaemia.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coronary syndromes
set1.q: How are the coronary syndromes classified?
opts: By which coronary artery is involved
Vessel involvement is not the basis of the classification, which rests on the severity and onset of symptoms.
By the severity and onset of cardiac symptoms
Correct. The division is clinical rather than anatomical, which is why two syndromes with similar plaques sit in different categories. Into chronic and acute.
By the lipoprotein pattern of the patient
Lipoproteins relate to risk rather than to syndrome classification.
By the degree of luminal occlusion alone
Occlusion contributes, but the classification rests on severity and onset of symptoms.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: What happens to the valves as rheumatic endocardial inflammation progresses?
opts: Immediate calcification of the leaflets
Calcification is an age-related process rather than the rheumatic sequence.
Swelling and erosion first
Correct. The scarring is what remains decades later, and it is why rheumatic fever appears as a cause of stenosis. Then scarring and shortening of the valvular structures.
Ballooning of the leaflets into the atrium
That describes prolapse. Rheumatic inflammation produces swelling and erosion, then scarring and shortening.
Rupture of the papillary muscles
Papillary rupture is a cause of acute regurgitation rather than the rheumatic sequence.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: What is a prerequisite for infective endocarditis?
opts: Pre-existing calcification of the valve
Pre-existing valve pathology matters for the subacute form, but bloodstream invasion is the prerequisite.
Invasion of the bloodstream by the organism
Correct. The valve is reached through the blood, so bacteraemia has to come first.
A recent myocardial infarction
Infarction is not a prerequisite. Invasion of the bloodstream is, since the valve is reached through the blood.
Immune cross-reactivity with streptococcal antigens
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. Infective endocarditis requires bloodstream invasion by the organism.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: What is a vegetation?
opts: Microorganisms enmeshed in fibrin deposits
Correct. As they enlarge they interfere with valve function and predispose to embolism, so the lesion does harm in two distinct ways.
A calcified nodule on the valve annulus
Vegetations are organisms within fibrin rather than calcific nodules.
A ballooned segment of valve leaflet
That describes prolapse. A vegetation is microorganisms enmeshed in fibrin deposits on the valve.
A thrombus within the left atrial appendage
Atrial clot relates to atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: Why does the heart compensate well for a slowly progressive stenosis?
opts: It hypertrophies its myocardial cells as the gradient develops
Correct. Slow progression allows the adaptation, which is why such valves can be severely narrowed before anything is noticed.
It dilates the affected chamber immediately
Dilation is the response to volume overload rather than to pressure overload from stenosis.
It develops collateral circulation across the valve
Collaterals form around coronary obstruction rather than across a valve.
It reduces the heart rate permanently
Rate reduction is not the described compensation. The heart compensates by myocardial cell hypertrophy as the gradient develops.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: By what mechanism does rheumatic fever damage the heart?
opts: An immune attack arising from cross-reactivity after streptococcal infection
Correct. The organism is long gone; what damages the heart is the immune response aimed at something that resembles it.
Direct invasion of the valve leaflets by the organism
Direct invasion describes infective endocarditis rather than rheumatic disease.
Calcium deposition on the leaflets
Calcification is an age-related process rather than the rheumatic mechanism.
Ischaemic necrosis of the papillary muscles
Papillary necrosis is a consequence of infarction rather than of rheumatic fever.

set1.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set1.q: What happens once the injured endothelium becomes more permeable?
opts: Calcium is deposited directly into the media
Calcification is not the step that follows increased permeability.
Leukocytes are recruited and low density lipoprotein leaks through to be oxidised
Correct. The lipid has to get into the wall before it can do harm, and the increased permeability is what lets it.
Smooth muscle cells migrate out of the vessel wall
Smooth muscle proliferates within the wall rather than migrating out of it.
The vessel dilates to preserve flow
Dilation is not the described response to endothelial injury here.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
set1.q: Where are nearly all myocardial infarcts located, and which artery is most often responsible?
opts: The right ventricle, most often the right coronary artery
Nearly all infarcts are in the left ventricular walls, and the left anterior descending accounts for the largest share.
The left ventricular walls, most often the left anterior descending
Correct. The left ventricle does the pressure work, so it is the chamber whose supply matters most, and one artery accounts for the largest share.
The atria, most often the circumflex
The infarcts described are ventricular rather than atrial, and the left anterior descending supplies the largest share.
The interventricular septum only, most often the circumflex
The left anterior descending accounts for the largest share, and the infarcts are not confined to the septum.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: What happens in mitral regurgitation?
opts: Blood flows from atrium to ventricle during systole
That is the normal direction of flow, and it occurs during diastole.
Blood leaks from the aorta into the ventricle during diastole
That describes aortic regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation sends blood back into the atrium during systole.
Flow across the valve is obstructed during diastole
Obstruction during diastole describes mitral stenosis. Regurgitation is backflow into the atrium during systole.
Blood flows back from ventricle to atrium during systole
Correct, and because the leak occurs during systole, part of every beat is wasted going the wrong way. Raising left atrial volume and pressure.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
set1.q: Which factors are associated with dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Alcohol, genetics, pregnancy and a post-viral state
Correct. Four causes with nothing obvious in common, which is why the condition is grouped by what the ventricle does rather than by what caused it.
Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is given in relation to restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Aortic valve calcification
Valve calcification produces stenosis rather than dilated cardiomyopathy.
Streptococcal cross-reactivity
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. Dilated cardiomyopathy is associated with alcohol, genetics, pregnancy and a post-viral state.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set1.q: What is the mechanism of cardiac tamponade?
opts: Fibrous encasement of the heart developing over years
That describes constrictive pericarditis rather than tamponade.
Adhesion of the heart to surrounding mediastinal structures
That describes adhesive mediastinopericarditis. Tamponade is external compression by fluid, impairing filling.
Failure of the ventricle to contract because of inflammation
The impairment is of filling rather than of contraction: the chambers are compressed from outside by the fluid.
External compression of the chambers by pericardial fluid
Correct. The heart is prevented from filling from outside, so the muscle and valves may be entirely normal while the output collapses. Impairing filling.

set1.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set1.q: What do the macrophages within a plaque release, and with what effect?
opts: Collagen and fibrin, which stabilise the plaque
Collagen and fibrin form the stabilising cap later, and are not what the macrophages release here.
Enzymes that clear the lipid core entirely
The lipid accumulates rather than being cleared; the macrophages release inflammatory mediators and growth factor instead.
Inflammatory mediators and growth factor

Correct. This is the step that makes the lesion self-sustaining: the cells that arrived to deal with the lipid recruit more cells and more wall growth. Attracting more leukocytes and stimulating smooth muscle proliferation.
Vasodilators that increase flow through the vessel
Vasodilation is not the described consequence. The mediators recruit more leukocytes and stimulate smooth muscle proliferation.

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes for angina pectoris
set1.q: What is the mechanism of stable, typical angina?
opts: Vasospasm occurring unpredictably at rest
That describes Prinzmetal, variant angina. Stable angina follows a fixed stenosis and rising workload.
Plaque rupture with acute thrombosis
That is the mechanism of the acute coronary syndromes. Stable angina arises from a fixed stenosis under increased demand.
Stenotic vessels reduce flow to a critical level
Correct. The narrowing is fixed, so it is the rise in demand that precipitates each episode -- which is why the attacks are predictable. So perfusion fails under increased workload.
Inflammation of the pericardium limiting filling
That is constrictive pericardial disease rather than angina.

set1.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set1.q: What is the significance of a large lipid core within a plaque?
opts: A large core makes the plaque more stable
The opposite is described: a large lipid core makes the plaque fragile and liable to rupture.
A large core prevents platelet aggregation
Rupture of such a plaque exposes subendothelial proteins and initiates platelet aggregation.
A large core indicates the plaque has been cleared
The core is accumulated lipid and debris rather than evidence of clearance.
Plaques with large lipid cores are fragile and rupture
Correct. Size and stability run in opposite directions, which is why the dangerous plaque is not necessarily the one narrowing the lumen most.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: How does valvular stenosis change the work the heart does?
opts: It imposes extra VOLUME work, since blood returns across the valve
Extra volume work is what regurgitation imposes. Stenosis imposes pressure work, forcing blood through a smaller opening.
It reduces the work of the heart by limiting flow
Restricting the opening increases rather than reduces the work required.
It imposes extra PRESSURE work
Correct. This is the distinction that organises the whole valve section, and it predicts which chamber hypertrophies. Since blood must be forced through a smaller opening.
It has no haemodynamic effect until the valve is completely closed
Haemodynamics are affected once about half the opening is lost.

set1.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set1.q: How do the capillaries within the atherosclerotic arterial wall contribute to disruption?
opts: They deliver macrophages that dissolve the fibrous cap
Bleeding and pressure build-up is the described mechanism rather than cap dissolution.
They drain lipid out of the core, collapsing the plaque
The described consequence is deposition and pressure rather than drainage.
Their thin walls bleed
Correct. The plaque can be disrupted from the inside as well as from the lumen, which is a route easy to overlook. Depositing blood products and raising pressure within the plaque.
They constrict, producing local ischaemia within the wall
Constriction of these capillaries is not the described mechanism.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: Why does aortic stenosis predispose the heart to ischaemia and angina?
opts: The stenotic valve obstructs the coronary ostia directly
Direct ostial obstruction is not the mechanism. Hypertrophy and high ventricular pressures raise demand beyond supply.
Hypertrophy and high ventricular pressures raise demand beyond what supply can meet
Correct. Angina can arise with entirely normal coronary arteries, because the problem is on the demand side of the same equation.
The ventricle dilates and thins, reducing perfusion
The ventricle hypertrophies rather than dilating, and that hypertrophy is what raises oxygen demand.
Calcium emboli lodge in the coronary arteries
Embolism from the valve is not the mechanism. Hypertrophy and high pressures predispose the heart to ischaemia.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set1.q: What are the primary causes of valvular stenosis?
opts: Post-inflammatory scarring from rheumatic fever
Correct. One is an immune injury from decades earlier and the other is simple wear, which is why the two produce stenosis in very different age groups. Valvular calcification with ageing.
Infective endocarditis and papillary muscle rupture
These cause regurgitation rather than stenosis. Stenosis follows rheumatic scarring or valvular calcification with ageing.
Homocysteine-induced vascular injury
That mechanism relates to atherosclerosis rather than to valves.
Coxsackievirus infection of the valve leaflets
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Stenosis follows rheumatic scarring or age-related calcification.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
set1.q: What defines dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: A thickened, hyperkinetic ventricular muscle mass
That describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The dilated form is cardiac failure with dilation of one or both ventricles.
A stiff, fibrotic ventricle with impaired filling
That describes restrictive cardiomyopathy. The dilated form is failure with dilation of one or both ventricles.
Cardiac failure with dilation of one or both ventricular chambers
Correct. It is named for the chamber change, and the causes listed for it are otherwise unrelated to one another.
Inflammation with leukocyte infiltration and necrosis
That describes myocarditis. Dilated cardiomyopathy is cardiac failure with chamber dilation.

set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of common cardiopathies
set1.q: What properties make homocysteine harmful to vessels?
opts: It is atherogenic but protects against thrombosis
It promotes thrombosis rather than protecting against it; its properties are described as both atherogenic and prothrombotic.
It raises low density lipoprotein production in the liver
Its described properties are direct vascular injury and thrombosis rather than an effect on lipoprotein production.
It inhibits smooth muscle proliferation
Smooth muscle hypertrophy is among the injuries it causes, so it does not inhibit that process.
It is atherogenic and prothrombotic
Correct. Two harms at once: it damages the wall and it promotes clot on that damaged wall, which is the same one-two that drives coronary events generally.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
set1.q: Why is a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy symptomatic?
opts: Reduced contractility of a thin, dilated ventricle
The muscle mass is thickened and hyperkinetic rather than thin and weak.
Fibrosis restricting filling
Fibrosis restricting filling describes restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Backflow across an incompetent aortic valve
That describes aortic regurgitation. Symptoms in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy come from outflow obstruction and impaired filling.
Ventricular outflow obstruction and impaired diastolic filling
Correct. The thickened muscle obstructs the way out and stiffens the chamber, so both halves of the cycle suffer.

set1.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
set1.q: Which determinants of workload increase myocardial oxygen demand?
opts: Heart rate, preload, afterload and contractility
Correct. Raising any one of the four raises demand, which is why ischaemia can appear with the coronary anatomy entirely unchanged.
Coronary perfusion pressure and collateral circulation
These are supply-side factors rather than determinants of demand.
Plaque size and composition
These affect supply rather than the work the heart is doing.
Serum lipoprotein concentration
Lipoproteins relate to plaque formation rather than to moment-to-moment oxygen demand.

set1.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set1.q: At what degree of occlusion is blood flow described as compromised?
opts: Twenty-five per cent
Flow is not described as compromised at this degree of narrowing.
Fifty per cent
Fifty per cent is the figure given for haemodynamic effect in valvular stenosis, not for coronary occlusion.
Ninety-five per cent
Flow is described as compromised well before this, at about seventy-five per cent occlusion.
Seventy-five per cent
Correct. It takes a great deal of narrowing before flow suffers, which is why plaques grow silently for years.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set1.q: What produces adhesive mediastinopericarditis?
opts: Suppurative or caseous pericarditis
Correct. The cardiac workload rises because the heart is now working against the structures it is stuck to. Or surgery, destroying the sac so the heart adheres to surrounding structures.
Fluid accumulating without inflammation
That describes a pericardial effusion. The adhesive form follows suppurative or caseous pericarditis, or surgery.
A dense, non-elastic sac encasing the heart
That describes constrictive pericarditis. In the adhesive form the sac is destroyed and the heart adheres to surrounding structures.
Immune cross-reactivity after streptococcal infection
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. The adhesive form follows suppurative or caseous pericarditis, or surgery.

set1.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
set1.q: What is the immediate metabolic consequence of reduced oxygen supply to cardiac cells?
opts: The formation of adenosine triphosphate falls
Correct. The cell loses its energy currency first, and everything that follows -- failure to contract, then death -- is downstream of that.
Lactate is converted back into glucose within the cell
The described consequence is a fall in energy production rather than gluconeogenesis.
Calcium is actively pumped out of the cell more rapidly
Active transport requires the energy that is now in short supply.
Oxygen extraction from the blood falls
Extraction is not the described first consequence; the shortfall is in supply relative to demand.

set1.io: Review the different lipoproteins
set1.q: What distinguishes very low density lipoprotein from low density lipoprotein?
opts: It is high in cholesterol and decreases risk
It is high in triglycerides, and it increases rather than decreases risk.
It carries cholesterol back to the liver
That is the role of high density lipoprotein, and it is why high density lipoprotein lowers rather than raises risk.
It is not associated with atherosclerotic risk
It is described as increasing risk, through the triglycerides it carries rather than through cholesterol.
It is high in triglycerides rather than cholesterol
Correct. Both raise risk, so the distinction to hold is what each is carrying rather than which direction it pushes risk. Increases risk.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
set2.q: What defines coronary heart disease?
opts: Failure of the myocardium to contract because of intrinsic muscle disease
That describes a cardiomyopathy. Coronary heart disease is a problem of blood supply to muscle that is itself capable of working.
Inflammation of the coronary arteries with leukocyte infiltration
Inflammation participates in plaque formation, but the disease is defined by inadequate oxygen delivery rather than by inflammation itself.
Obstruction of venous drainage from the myocardium
The problem is arterial supply. Venous drainage is not the mechanism described.
Insufficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the myocardium because of atherosclerotic vessels
Correct. The definition is about supply failing rather than about pain or any particular syndrome, which is why so many different presentations sit underneath it.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: What sequence follows the raised left atrial pressure of mitral stenosis?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy, then left sided failure
The obstruction is upstream of the left ventricle, which is underfilled rather than overloaded.
Aortic root dilation
Root dilation causes aortic regurgitation. Mitral stenosis leads to atrial enlargement and pulmonary hypertension.
Atrial enlargement and hypertrophy

Correct. A valve on the left side of the heart ends by failing the right side, because the pressure has nowhere to go but backwards through the lungs. Raised pulmonary pressures, then right sided hypertrophy and failure.
Pericardial effusion and tamponade
Pericardial fluid accumulation is a separate process. Mitral stenosis backs pressure up through the lungs to the right heart.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
set2.q: What pattern of chamber involvement occurs in myocarditis?
opts: Left ventricular dysfunction with general dilation of all four chambers
Correct. The dysfunction is focused on the left ventricle while the dilation is general, which is a combination worth holding.
Isolated right ventricular hypertrophy
That pattern follows chronic pulmonary hypertension in mitral stenosis.
Left atrial enlargement alone
Atrial enlargement alone describes mitral valve disease. Myocarditis dilates all four chambers with left ventricular dysfunction.
No chamber change, with inflammation confined to the endocardium
The endocardial structures are usually normal, and the chambers do dilate.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: What is the central haemodynamic abnormality in mitral stenosis?
opts: An abnormal gradient during systole
The mitral valve is open during diastole, so the gradient appears then.
An abnormal left atrial to left ventricular pressure gradient during diastole
Correct. The atrium stays at higher pressure than the ventricle through diastole, and the gradient widens as the stenosis worsens.
Backflow from the ventricle into the atrium during systole
That describes mitral regurgitation. Mitral stenosis produces an atrial to ventricular gradient during diastole.
Obstruction to outflow from the left ventricle
That describes aortic stenosis. Mitral stenosis obstructs filling and produces a diastolic gradient.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set2.q: How does pericardial disease usually arise?
opts: As a primary condition in most cases
It is rarely primary; it is usually secondary to another cause, with fluid accumulating and painful inflammation of the pericardial structures.
Only as a consequence of myocardial infarction
Infarction is one possible primary cause among many rather than the only route.
Secondary to another primary cause
Correct. It is usually a manifestation of something else, and whatever the cause, fluid accumulates and the pericardial structures become painfully inflamed. Rarely as a primary condition.
Only from direct infection of the pericardium
Causes are various rather than confined to infection, and pericardial disease is usually secondary to another primary cause.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
set2.q: How does an infarcted area change over the weeks that follow?
opts: It is replaced by functioning muscle within two weeks
Muscle is not regenerated. Necrotic tissue is removed by one to two weeks and replaced by tough fibrous scar by six.
Pale within a day

Correct. The sequence runs from removal of dead muscle to replacement by scar, and the scar does not contract. Then yellowish and soft with a red border, necrotic tissue removed by one to two weeks, tough fibrous scar by six.
It calcifies within forty-eight hours
Calcification is not the described sequence. The area pales within a day, then softens, and becomes fibrous scar by six weeks.
It remains unchanged indefinitely
The area passes through a defined sequence of change ending in scar.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: What happens to left ventricular stroke volume in mitral stenosis?
opts: It decreases
Correct. The ventricle is not diseased; it is simply not being filled, which is why the problem is upstream of it.
It increases to compensate
Reduced filling means the ventricle cannot raise its stroke volume.
It is unchanged until the valve closes completely
Stroke volume falls as the gradient worsens, because the ventricle is not being filled.
It becomes dependent on atrial contraction alone
The described consequence is a decreased left ventricular stroke volume, from inadequate filling.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
set2.q: At what point does myocardium become ischaemic?
opts: When metabolic demand for oxygen exceeds supply
Correct. It is a relationship rather than a threshold, which is why ischaemia can arise either from supply falling or from demand rising with the supply unchanged.
When coronary blood flow falls below a fixed absolute value
No absolute flow figure defines it; what matters is flow relative to what the muscle is demanding at that moment.
Only once a coronary artery is completely occluded
Complete occlusion is one route to it, but ischaemia begins well before that whenever demand outruns supply.
Only when the patient experiences chest pain
Pain is a symptom that may or may not appear; ischaemia is defined by the supply and demand mismatch itself.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
set2.q: What is the initiating feature of myocardial infarction?
opts: Gradual narrowing of the lumen over years
Gradual narrowing produces stable angina and allows collaterals to develop.
Vasospasm of an angiographically normal artery
Vasospasm is the mechanism of variant angina rather than the initiating feature of infarction.
Inflammation of the pericardium
Pericardial inflammation is a separate disease process. Infarction begins with thrombosis on a cracked plaque.
Thrombosis on an ulcerated or cracked atherosclerotic plaque
Correct. The plaque has to fail before the thrombus forms, which is why plaque stability matters more than plaque size.

set2.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
set2.q: Why does slowly progressive plaque formation allow the heart to tolerate more narrowing?
opts: The myocardium reduces its oxygen demand permanently
Demand is not described as falling; an alternative supply route develops instead.
Collateral circulation develops over the years the plaque is growing
Correct. Time is what permits the adaptation, which is also why an abrupt occlusion in a previously healthy vessel can do more damage than a severe chronic stenosis.
The plaque itself becomes permeable to blood
Plaques do not conduct blood through themselves. Collateral vessels develop around the obstruction over the years it takes to form.
Cardiac cells switch to anaerobic metabolism indefinitely
Indefinite anaerobic metabolism is not the described adaptation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set2.q: How does constrictive pericarditis impair the heart?
opts: The sac fills rapidly with fluid, compressing the chambers
Rapid fluid accumulation describes tamponade. In the constrictive form a scarred, non-elastic sac encases the heart.
The heart adheres to surrounding mediastinal structures
That describes the adhesive form. In the constrictive form the sac becomes dense and fibrous, encasing the heart like a stiff cage.
The sac becomes dense

Correct, and the result resembles restrictive cardiomyopathy in that filling is what fails -- but the stiffness here is outside the muscle rather than within it. Non-elastic and scarred, encasing the heart and impairing diastolic filling.
The myocardium becomes fibrotic and non-compliant
Fibrosis within the myocardium describes restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
set2.q: On what does the result of vessel occlusion depend?
opts: Collateral circulation
Correct. The same occlusion in two hearts produces different damage, which is why the vessel alone does not predict the outcome. Workload and the length of time.
The lipoprotein pattern of the patient
Lipoproteins relate to plaque formation rather than to the consequence of an occlusion.
Which valve is nearest the occluded segment
Valve proximity is not a determinant. The result depends on collateral circulation, workload and how long the occlusion lasts.
The presence of pericardial fluid
Pericardial fluid is not a determinant here. Collateral circulation, workload and duration are what decide the result.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
set2.q: What are the consequences of myocardial ischaemia?
opts: Abnormal rhythm only, with function preserved throughout
Function is affected as well; the ischaemic myocardium cannot contract normally.
Abnormal heart function and abnormal rhythm
Correct. Two immediate consequences and one that depends on duration, which is why time is the variable that decides how much muscle is lost. With irreversible damage if prolonged.
Immediate irreversible damage in every case
Damage becomes irreversible only if the ischaemia is prolonged; brief ischaemia does not kill the cell.
Valvular incompetence as the first consequence
Valve function is not the described consequence of myocardial ischaemia.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: What is the difference between valvular stenosis and regurgitation?
opts: Stenosis is failure to close, regurgitation is failure to open
The definitions are the other way round: stenosis is failure to open completely, regurgitation failure to close completely.
Both describe failure of the valve to open
They describe opposite failures: stenosis is failure to open, regurgitation failure to close.
Stenosis is failure to open completely, regurgitation is failure to close completely
Correct, and the consequence follows directly: one makes the heart push harder, the other makes it push more.
Stenosis affects only the mitral valve and regurgitation only the aortic
Both can affect either valve. The distinction is between failing to open and failing to close.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set2.q: A serosanguinous pericardial effusion is secondary to which causes?
opts: Heart failure and hypoproteinaemia together
These produce a serous transudate rather than a serosanguinous effusion.
Blunt trauma, cardiac surgery or resuscitation
Correct. All three involve mechanical force on the chest, which is what puts blood into what would otherwise be a serous fluid.
Obstruction to lymphatic drainage alone
Lymphatic obstruction produces a chylous effusion. The serosanguinous type follows blunt trauma, surgery or resuscitation.
Penetrating cardiac trauma only
Penetrating trauma produces frank blood in the sac, a haemopericardium.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: Why does atrial fibrillation develop in mitral stenosis?
opts: The ventricle hypertrophies and compresses the conducting system
Ventricular hypertrophy is not the described mechanism here.
Coronary ischaemia damages the sinus node
Ischaemic damage to the node is not the described mechanism.
Pericardial inflammation spreads to the atrium
Pericardial disease is not the cause. The atrium fibrillates because it enlarges as its volume and pressure rise.
The atrium enlarges as its volume rises
Correct, and the enlarged fibrillating atrium then predisposes to clot within it, which is the next consequence in the chain.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: How do the chambers compensate in mitral regurgitation?
opts: The ventricle hypertrophies without dilating
Hypertrophy without dilation is the response to pressure overload from stenosis.
The atrium shrinks to limit the regurgitant volume
The atrium dilates rather than shrinking, and hypertrophies, as does the ventricle.
Both atrium and ventricle dilate and hypertrophy to handle the extra volume
Correct. Volume work produces dilation alongside hypertrophy, as against the hypertrophy alone that pressure work produces.
Neither chamber changes until failure occurs
Both chambers dilate and hypertrophy to handle the extra volume before failure supervenes.

set2.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
set2.q: Which factors are described as impairing coronary perfusion?
opts: Plaques, thrombosis, vasospasm, microcirculation, pressure
Correct. Five different ways to arrive at the same shortfall, only one of which is the fixed narrowing people picture first.
Increased heart rate and contractility, acting alone
These raise demand rather than impairing supply; they are on the workload side.
Valvular stenosis and regurgitation, acting alone
Valve disease increases cardiac workload rather than impairing coronary perfusion directly.
Pericardial inflammation
Pericardial disease is not among the described causes of impaired coronary perfusion.

set2.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set2.q: Which are given as causes of the initiating endothelial injury?
opts: Wall stress, toxins, inflammation, hyperlipidaemia
Correct. Mechanical, chemical, inflammatory and metabolic insults all converge on the same first step, which is why so many different risk factors end in the same lesion.
Valvular calcification and rheumatic scarring
These damage valves rather than injuring coronary endothelium.
Viral infection of the myocardium
That relates to myocarditis rather than to endothelial injury.
Pericardial inflammation
Pericardial disease does not injure coronary endothelium in the way described.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
set2.q: Atherosclerosis narrows the coronary lumen. Which processes does that narrowing predispose to?
opts: Valvular calcification and regurgitation
Valve disease is a separate process and is not a consequence of coronary narrowing.
Pericardial effusion and tamponade
Pericardial disease is not precipitated by coronary narrowing.
Myocardial leukocyte infiltration and necrosis without vessel involvement
That describes myocarditis, which is not a consequence of coronary atherosclerosis.
Thrombosis, coronary vasospasm and endothelial cell dysfunction
Correct. The narrowing is the setting rather than the whole disease: what precipitates an event is one of these three acting on an already narrowed vessel.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: At what degree of closure does stenosis begin to affect haemodynamics?
opts: About ten per cent
Haemodynamic effect is described from about fifty per cent closure onwards.
About fifty per cent
Correct. It is a lower threshold than the seventy-five per cent that compromises coronary flow, and the two figures are easy to swap.
About seventy-five per cent
Seventy-five per cent is the coronary occlusion figure rather than the valvular one.
Only at complete closure
Effects appear well before complete closure, from about fifty per cent.

set2.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set2.q: What determines the risk that a plaque will rupture?
opts: Its age alone
Age is not given as the determinant; composition and mechanical stress are.
Its composition
Correct. Two factors, one internal and one external, which is why an identical plaque may be stable in one vessel and not in another. The mechanical stresses acting on it.
The degree of luminal narrowing alone
Severe stenosis is one of the vulnerability features, but composition and stress are what determine rupture risk.
The lipoprotein that delivered the lipid
Which lipoprotein delivered the lipid is not described as determining rupture.

set2.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set2.q: What initiates atherosclerotic plaque formation?
opts: Deposition of calcium on the intimal surface
Calcification is a feature of established disease rather than the initiating event.
Rupture of the vasa vasorum within the arterial wall
Haemorrhage from those capillaries contributes to plaque rupture later, not to initiation.
Platelet aggregation on an intact endothelium
Platelet aggregation follows exposure of subendothelial proteins, which requires the endothelium to be damaged first.
Injury to the endothelial cells of the vessel
Correct. Everything that follows -- permeability, leukocytes, oxidised lipid, foam cells -- is downstream of that first injury.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: Which organisms most commonly cause infective endocarditis?
opts: Streptococcal strains and Staphylococcus aureus
Correct. The same two names recur, with the less virulent organisms reserved for the subacute form on an already damaged valve.
Coxsackievirus and adenovirus
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Endocarditis is most often streptococcal strains or Staphylococcus aureus.
Candida alone
Candida appears among the less virulent causes of the subacute form rather than as the commonest cause.
Group A streptococcus through immune cross-reactivity
Cross-reactivity is the rheumatic mechanism rather than direct infection.

set2.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
set2.q: Which are listed as PROBABLE rather than major risk factors?
opts: Hypertension, diabetes and obesity
All three are in the major category. The probable ones are male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein.
Age and family history
Both are major risk factors, and they are the two that cannot be altered. The probable list is male sex, homocysteine and C reactive protein.
Abnormal lipids and cigarette smoking
Both are major risk factors. The probable ones are male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein.
Male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein
Correct. Two of the three are laboratory measurements rather than clinical facts, which is part of why they sit in the weaker category.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: Why does a high afterload worsen mitral regurgitation?
opts: It reduces left atrial pressure
Atrial pressure rises with regurgitation rather than falling.
It prevents the ventricle from dilating
Dilation occurs as compensation for the extra volume. A high afterload increases the amount regurgitated.
It increases the amount of blood regurgitated
Correct. The ventricle takes the path of least resistance, so the harder it is to eject forwards, the more goes backwards.
It converts the regurgitation into stenosis
Afterload does not change the lesion; it increases the proportion of each beat that goes backwards.

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes for angina pectoris
set2.q: What distinguishes angina pectoris from infarction at the cellular level?
opts: The ischaemia affects only the right ventricle
Location is not what separates them. Angina is ischaemia intermittent and insufficient to kill cardiac cells.
There is no ischaemia, only abnormal conduction
Angina is defined by ischaemia; what distinguishes it is that the ischaemia stops short of killing cells.
The ischaemia is intermittent and insufficient to kill cardiac cells
Correct. Same mechanism, different endpoint: the supply falls short but recovers before the cells are lost.
Cell death occurs but is confined to the endocardium
Cell death is precisely what angina does not produce; that is what separates it from infarction.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
set2.q: What is restrictive cardiomyopathy most often related to?
opts: Alcohol and pregnancy
These are factors in dilated cardiomyopathy. The restrictive form is usually related to a specific condition such as amyloidosis.
A specific clinical condition
Correct. It is usually secondary to something identifiable, unlike the other two patterns which are more often idiopathic. Such as amyloidosis.
Coxsackievirus infection
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is most often secondary to a condition such as amyloidosis.
Ageing valvular calcification
Calcification produces valvular stenosis rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
set2.q: Which effusion type follows heart failure or hypoproteinaemia?
opts: A chylous collection
Chylous fluid follows obstruction to lymphatic drainage. Heart failure and hypoproteinaemia produce a serous transudate.
A haemopericardium
Frank blood follows penetrating cardiac trauma. Heart failure and hypoproteinaemia produce a serous transudate.
A serosanguinous effusion
That follows blunt trauma, surgery or resuscitation. Heart failure and hypoproteinaemia produce a serous transudate.
A serous transudate
Correct. Both causes act by altering the forces governing fluid movement rather than by injuring anything.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
set2.q: What is the haemodynamic consequence of aortic stenosis?
opts: Obstruction to outflow during systole
Correct. The aortic valve is open during systole, so this is when the obstruction bites. With a pressure gradient across the valve during ejection.
Obstruction to filling during diastole
Obstruction during diastole describes mitral stenosis. Aortic stenosis obstructs outflow during systole.
Backflow into the ventricle during diastole
That is aortic regurgitation. Aortic stenosis obstructs outflow during systole, with a gradient across the valve.
Backflow into the atrium during systole
That is mitral regurgitation. Aortic stenosis produces a ventricular to aortic gradient during ejection.
